\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{जीरकम्} (jīrakam)}{जीरकम् (jīrakam)}]{\sk{जीरकम्} (jīrakam) — cumin}

\label{lesson:SA-C159-jirakam}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a small lamp, then the Sanskrit for a door panel, a shutter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{जीरकम्}}
\textbf{\sk{जीरकम्}} — \emph{jīrakam} — \textquotedblleft{}cumin\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{jīraka} \textquotedblleft{}cumin seed\textquotedblright{} is a word of the medical writer Suśruta, and neither MW nor CDIAL 5234 gives a derivation, so its origin is uncertain. It lives on as Hindi and Bengali \emph{jīrā} and Gujarati \emph{jīrũ} \textquotedblleft{}cumin\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 5234).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]

\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{सर्षपः} (sarṣapaḥ)}{सर्षपः (sarṣapaḥ)}]{\sk{सर्षपः} (sarṣapaḥ) — mustard}

\label{lesson:SA-C159-sarsapah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a door panel, a shutter, then the Sanskrit for cumin.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{सर्षपः}}
\textbf{\sk{सर्षपः}} — \emph{sarṣapaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}mustard\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sarṣapa} \textquotedblleft{}mustard, mustard seed\textquotedblright{} goes back to the Ṣaḍviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (CDIAL 13281). Its origin is uncertain: DEDR 921, citing Burrow and Mayrhofer, discusses a possible link with Dravidian words for mustard.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{हिंगु} (hiṅgu)}{हिंगु (hiṅgu)}]{\sk{हिंगु} (hiṅgu) — asafoetida}

\label{lesson:SA-C159-hingu}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for cumin, then the Sanskrit for mustard.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{हिंगु}}
\textbf{\sk{हिंगु}} — \emph{hiṅgu} — \textquotedblleft{}asafoetida\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{hiṅgu} \textquotedblleft{}asafoetida\textquotedblright{} appears from the Mahābhārata on. EtymDB lists it as borrowed from Iranian, but neither MW nor CDIAL 14079 gives a derivation, so its origin is not settled. It lives on as Punjabi \emph{hiṅg} and Hindi \emph{hīṅg} (CDIAL 14079).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{तिलः} (tilaḥ)}{तिलः (tilaḥ)}]{\sk{तिलः} (tilaḥ) — sesame}

\label{lesson:SA-C159-tilah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for mustard, then the Sanskrit for asafoetida.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{तिलः}}
\textbf{\sk{तिलः}} — \emph{tilaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}sesame\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tila} \textquotedblleft{}sesame\textquotedblright{} is old, in the Atharvaveda, and is probably borrowed from Munda: CDIAL 5827 follows Kuiper and thinks a Dravidian source less likely. It lives on as Hindi and Punjabi \emph{til} (CDIAL 5827).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{चणकः} (caṇakaḥ)}{चणकः (caṇakaḥ)}]{\sk{चणकः} (caṇakaḥ) — a chickpea}

\label{lesson:SA-C159-canakah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for asafoetida, then the Sanskrit for sesame.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{चणकः}}
\textbf{\sk{चणकः}} — \emph{caṇakaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a chickpea\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{caṇaka} is \emph{caṇa} \textquotedblleft{}the chickpea\textquotedblright{} with the suffix \emph{-ka} (CDIAL 4579). Neither MW nor CDIAL gives a derivation for \emph{caṇa}, so its origin is uncertain. It lives on as Hindi and Punjabi \emph{canā}, \emph{caṇā} (CDIAL 4579).
\end{cousinweb}

\end{grammarlens}
